messages.body_plain:
Dear team,

I'm trying to implement rjmcmc in my models. It's very easy to modify the code for this purpose, thanks to the tutorial. However, I'm still not entirely sure what I should do. Say I have the following model:

y[i] = z[1] * beta[1] + z[2] * beta[2] * x1[i] + z[3] * beta[3] * x2[i] + epsilon[i]

Do I simply run the model to fully explore the parameter space, and use beta values when the corresponding z equals 1 to represent its posterior distribution, or do I run the model first and select beta's based on the inclusion probability, and then run a reduced model with selected beta's only, without z, to get the posteriors of beta's? If the latter, is there a recommended cutoff value for the inclusion probability to select beta's?

Best,
Qing

messages.body_plain:
hi Qing,

The danger in running an initial model and then, based on that, running a reduced model is that you're using the data twice, so you're doing what statisticians call "post-selection inference".
I would say that in reporting results you would use the model to fully explore the parameter space and report the posterior inclusion probabilities of individual betas, or groups of betas, as well as reporting the posteriors for the betas conditional on a beta being in the model as well.

Also, it may be that two betas trade off with each other because their x's are correlated. E.g., the posterior probability that beta[1] is in the model might be around 0.5 and the same for beta[2], but the posterior probability that one of them is in the model might be near 1. So that is something to keep in mind.

Others may have thoughts as well.

-chris

hi Harry, I think the problem is that you're trying to use a fork-based cluster. We have some discussion of this in our example on parallelizing NIMBLE. Please try the ideas there (either not using forking or making sure to set up separate temp directories for the processes) and let me know if that doesn't solve the problem.

-chris

I ran into this issue doing some population modelling. I had a part of my model with something like n_{t+1} ~ dbinom(p, n_t) where the n's are both latent stochastic nodes.  I tried a few things that failed which I'll list below but in the end had some success just avoiding the slice sampler and writing my own sampler that guarantees any proposal n_{t+1} <= n_t.

Example code available here:
https://gist.github.com/ASeatonSpatial/03b958a1172c57823c9eda69ef29ecf5

The things that failed:

1. I tried avoiding discrete nodes all together by writing my own custom binomial distribution that allows non-integers (replacing the factorials in the binomial PMF with the gamma function).  My hope was whatever default sample got assigned here would handle it no problem.  This didn't work, I got repeated -Inf warnings and the mixing was very bad.  This made me think that the issue is proposing n_{t+1} > n_t or n_{t+1}<0, because that was the only way my custom distribution would return -Inf.

2. I tried using the inbuillt nimble truncation option: x ~ T(dbinom(p, n), 0, n) but got an error about cycles in the model graph.  Whatever this does by default for dbinom doesn't handle this use case.

That led me to try the above random walk sampler instead.

On Wednesday, November 29, 2023 at 6:03:53 PM UTC Abbey Feuka wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> I'm late to the party, but posting this for reference, in case anyone's in a similar situation. I had a similar problem to Ben and Matt where I was fitting a removal model using a Binomial likelihood (simplified pseudo-code for the relevant portion):
>
> y[i,t] ~ dbinom(p, N[i,t])
> delta[i,t] <- lambda[i,t] * (N[i,t-1] - y[i,t-1])
> N[i,t] ~ dPois(delta[i,t])
>
> and I was getting the same warning messages about the slice sampler reaching maximum contractions for N (latent population size). It was at weird values for N: as in super high or negative values. I realized it was an issue with both my prior distributions and initial values. Because the model removes individuals from the estimated N at each time step, I needed to specify initial values for N that were sufficiently high enough to not send it into the negatives when animals are removed. I also needed to rein in the priors and starting values for lambda (population growth) to ensure it's staying fairly tightly around 1, and again not sending the population skyrocketing or plummeting at each time step. This took a little bit of simulation because I specified lambda as a function of landscape covariates.

>

Hi Chris,

Sorry for my delayed answer.

Thanks a lot for your answer! Sorry I tried to be both clear and concise, but I ended up not being clear enough.

1)     Does each individual in each year have their own state? If so, what variable in your model represents that state? You index `x` by state (1 or 2) but I don't see in your email where you denote the unknown state. I would think there should be something like `s[i,t]` that is a discrete variable taking possible values 1,2,...,max_number_states.

Correct. There are 12 states including the dead state in this model.

2)     When you talk about transition probabilities, these are the probabilities of going from one state at time `t` to another state at time `t+1`, right? Is the 'state' that relates to the transition probabilities the same state you are talking about? If so, I would think you would have `beta[i, t, k1, k2]` indicating the probability of going from state k1 at time t to state k2 at time t+1 for individual i.

Yes, by transition probabilities I did mean the probabilities of going from one state at time ‘t’ to another state at time ‘t+1’. And this 'state' is the state I was talking about. It would indeed make more sense to write beta as ‘beta[i, t, k1, k2]’, though beta is only one of the components of the transition probabilities (which is a product of several probabilities, e.g. surviving * migrating * breeding *…).

3)     I would think that an individual in year t would have a single unknown migration date, i.e., X[i,t] rather than X[i,t,k]. That date might have a different distribution depending on the state the individual is in. Just to give an example, perhaps `X[i,t] ~ dnorm(mu_X[s[i,t]], sd=sigma)` where `s[i,t]` is the state of individual i in year t.

Hi Marwan,

I am still a bit confused here in terms of notation. In your email you ask about `mu_X[12]`, where `mu_X` has a single index, but in your original code `mu_X` has three indices.

Assuming that you mean to have a single index, then for any state in which migration can occur, it makes sense to have something like `X[i,t] ~ dnorm(mu_X[z[i,t]], sd=sigma)`. This specification says that the migration date for individual i at time t will be on average the `mu_X` value associated with the state that that individual is currently in, which is `z[i,t]`.

However for state 12 (death) (and some other states, as you say), migration can't occur. This means that if the MCMC proposes `z[i,t]=12`, it should also be proposing to remove `X[i,t]` from the model in some sense. And when it proposes to go from `z[i,t]=12` to some other value for `z[i,t]` it needs to propose a value for `X[i,t]` as it is reentering the model. This changes the dimension of the parameter space. In some cases folks use reversible jump MCMC for this, though the technical details can get complicated.

We have a reversible jump sampler for variable selection in regression problems, but I doubt that one could use it directly in this case.

I think the danger here in how you are trying to set things up is that `X[i,t]` is being treated as still in the model in proposing to move to `z[i,t]=12`.

Perhaps another way to think about this is to think about joint sampling for (X[i,t], Z[i,t]). If `Z[i,t]=12` is proposed, one also proposes to set `X[i,t]` to some "dummy" value, such as 99999, which has probability of 1 given `Z[i,t]=12`. Then if one proposes to set `Z[i,t]` to be something other than 12, one also proposes a value of `X[i,t]`, and acceptance depends on the joint density for the proposed `Z[i,t]` and `X[i,t]` values. This would involve setting up a user-defined specialized sampler and ensuring that it is a valid MCMC sampler.

It feels like others must have encountered such CR cases where one records other information about the captured individuals and wants to account for that in the modeling. I don't know this literature well, though.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
We're pleased to announce the release of version 1.3.0.

Version 1.3.0 provides some new and improved functionality, plus some bug fixes and improved error trapping.

The new and improved functionality includes:
A new multivariate MCMC sampler, the Barker proposal sampler (`sampler_barker`). We encourage users to try this sampler in place of the block Metropolis `RW_block` sampler and let us know how well it works. The Barker sampler uses gradient information and may improve adaptation behavior, including better mixing when parameters are on different scales or the initial proposal scale is too large.
An improved Laplace/AGHQ implementation that includes use of the `nlminb` optimizer for both inner and outer optimization (for better optimization performance), improved messaging and output naming, returning the log-likelihood and degrees of freedom for model selection calculations, and unified control of optimization method and other controls at either the build stage or through the `updateSettings` method.
The addition of the BOBYQA optimization method through `nimOptim`, registered via `nimOptimMethod`.
In addition to the new and improved functionality above, other bug fixes, improved error trapping, and enhancements include:
Preventing the use of nimbleFunction method names and nimbleFunction names that conflict with names in the nimble language (DSL).
More carefully checking for and warning of cases of NaN and non-finite log probability values in various samplers that in some cases may indicate invalid MCMC sampling.
More carefully handling of NaN and non-finite log probability values in the CRP sampler.
Error trapping cases of dynamic indices producing a non-scalar result in AD-enabled models and provide a suggested work-around.
Error trapping use of a non-existent `nimbleList`.
Preventing use of a single seed when running multiple chains via `runMCMC`.
Improving messaging related to lack of derivative support for functions.
Adding information about model macros to the manual.
Fixing bug in caching values in the CRP sampler when maximum number of clusters is exceeded, which would have caused incorrect sampling (albeit with the user having been warned that they should increase the maximum number of clusters).
Fixing an issue preventing use of `nimbleList` elements in `nimCat`.
Preventing an adaptation interval of one for various block samplers for which an interval of one leads to an error.
Allowing `runLaplace` to use an uncompiled Laplace object.
Please see the NEWS file <https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/devel/packages/nimble/inst/NEWS> in the installed package for more details.

- Chris Paciorek for the NIMBLE Development Team

messages.subject: [question] Updating SMC with new data?
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone!

I am trying to implement a state-space model and am interested in sequentially updating predictions as new data becomes available. My current approach uses a bootstrap filter (as shown in the example below), but I haven't found any examples or documentation on how to perform sequential updates efficiently. (I'm very new to Nimble so I don't even know if this is possible).

My specific question is: What is the recommended way to update a Nimble model and its associated particle filter (like bootstrapFilter) when new data points arrive sequentially (e.g., one observation per day)?

Thank you so much,

Rod

PS:

Here's a simplified example of my current setup:

library(nimble)
library(nimbleSMC)

# Define the state-space model
modelCode <- nimbleCode({
  # Priors
  sigma_state ~ dunif(0, 10)
  sigma_obs   ~ dunif(0, 10)
  x[1]        ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1)

  # State equation
  for(t in 2:50) {
    x[t] ~ dnorm(0.8 * x[t-1], sd = 1)
  }

  # Observation equation
  for(t in 1:50) {
    y[t] ~ dnorm(x[t], sd = 0.5)
  }
})

# Simulate data
set.seed(123)
true_x[1]        <- rnorm(1, 0, 1)
for(t in 2:50) {
  true_x[t] <- rnorm(1, 0.8 * true_x[t-1], 0.5)
}
y <- rnorm(50, true_x, 1)

# Create nimble model
data        <- list(y = c(y[1:45], rep(NA, 5))) # Include NA for missing data
constants <- list()
inits <- list(x = rep(0, 50), sigma_state = 1,  sigma_obs = 1)

model <- nimbleModel(modelCode,
                     constants = constants,
                     data = data,
                     inits = inits)

# Compile model
cModel <- compileNimble(model)

# Create and compile bootstrap filter
bf  <- buildBootstrapFilter(model,  nodes = 'x', control = list(saveAll = TRUE))
cBf <- compileNimble(bf, project = model)

# Run particle filter for initial data
nParticles <- 1000
cBf$run(nParticles)

# Get the results
boot_X <- as.matrix(cBf$mvEWSamples, 'x')

# Here I would like to update with a new observation efficiently
# For example, if y[46] becomes available:
new_y <- y[46]

# How to update the model and the filter efficiently with new_y?
# Is it possible to avoid rerunning the filter from scratch?

Hi Qing,

That is odd if you were able to run a shorter MCMC but not the longer one.

When we compile models or algorithms, we create a subdirectory called `nimble_generatedCode` within R's temp directory for the current R session. The path to R's temp directory can be found by running `tempdir()` in your R session.

1) So before you run `compileNimble(model,mcmc)`, you might check that `C:\Users\QING~1.ZHA\AppData\Local\Temp\Rtmpqs5udP` exists (but be careful when you do this to replace "Rtmpqs5udP" with the actual temp dir for your current R session).

2) After the error occurs, you might run `traceback()` and see if that gives any useful error messages.  Also check at this point if `C:\Users\QING~1.ZHA\AppData\Local\Temp\Rtmpqs5udP` exists.

3) As a work around, you might be able to set `dirName` in your call to `compileNimble` to point to some other directory that exists and see if Nimble is able to create `nimble_generatedCode` in that other directory. See `help(compileNimble)` for more details.

-chris

Hi Simon,
I ran your code and used to following to track down where the error occurs

m <- nimbleModel(model, inits = init, data = data, constants = cons)
options(error=recover)
cm <- compileNimble(m)

Please replace
dist <- c()
with
dist <- numeric(length=500)

and
sample <- c()
with
sample <- 0

c() isn't a valid way to initiate a variable in nimbleFunction programming, although it's not error-trapped very well.

With those changes, your model compiles for me. Let's hope those are the only problems.

Perry

messages.subject: Need for speed with PVA
messages.body_plain:
Hi Folks,
I have an Integrated Population Model (IPM) that I've turned into a Population Viability Analysis (PVA). The IPM is comprised of several submodels including: productivity, multi-state Cormack-Jolly-Seber mark-recapture, count data, and a population model. I can run the IPM in about 1-2 days, but when I project the model into the future (45 scenarios, 50 years) the model becomes intractible (>12 day runtime). So I'm looking for strategies on speeding up the model/simulations, especially if there are any obvious bottlenecks.

Here are a few things I've already tried to speed computation
(A) I've parallelized the chains for running on an HPC.
(B) I've added non-centered random effects - this sped convergence greatly
(C) I tried to add HMC on non-discrete portions of the model- this returns an error when I add buildDerivs=TRUE, maybe because of the dcat distribution with stochastic indexing (discussed here <https://groups.google.com/g/nimble-users/c/aopq131HYj8/m/1M58LWARAgAJ>).

Here are a few things I'm thinking about trying:
(1) Can I add posterior draws from the IPM to the PVA so parameters are already converged and just simulate from those for the PVA part? This would be easiest to implement and fastest. Is this possible?
(2) Reparameterize around computational bottlenecks to increase speed.
(3) Vectorize submodels- For example maybe vectorizing across individuals in the mark-recapture model.
(4) Add HMC by modifying the dcat distribution in the mark-recapture model. (See discussion <https://groups.google.com/g/nimble-users/c/aopq131HYj8/m/1M58LWARAgAJ>) or by some other way. Maybe use the nimble ecology package for this?
(5) Use nimble functions to speed computation- if so, where would this be most effective?
(6) Use moment matching of estimates from the IPM to simulate from the estimated parameters

#' @section prior_samples sampler:
#'
#' The prior_samples sampler uses a provided set of numeric values (\code{samples}) to define the prior distribution of one or more model nodes.  One every MCMC iteration, the prior_samples sampler takes value(s) from the numeric values provided, and stores these value(s) into the target model node(s).  This allows one to define the prior distribution of model parameters empirically, using a set of numeric \code{samples}, presumably obtained previously using MCMC.  The \code{target} node may be either a single scalar node (scalar case), or a collection of model nodes.
#'
#' The prior_samples sampler provides two options for selection of the value to use on each MCMC iteration.  The default behaviour is to take sequential values from the \code{samples} vector (scalar case), or in the case of multiple dimensions, sequential rows of the \code{samples} matrix are used.  The alternative behaviour, by setting the control argument \code{randomDraws = TRUE}, will instead use random draws from the \code{samples} vector (scalar case), or randomly selected rows of the \code{samples} matrix in the multidimensional case.
#'
#' If the default of sequential selection of values is used, and the number of MCMC iterations exceeds the length of the \code{samples} vector (scalar case) or the number of rows of the \code{samples} matrix, then \code{samples} will be recycled as necessary for the number of MCMC iterations.  A message to this effect is also printed at the beginning of the MCMC chain.
#'
#' Logically, prior_samples samplers might want to operate first, in advance of other samplers, on every MCMC iteration.  By default, at the time of MCMC building, all prior_samples samplers are re-ordered to appear first in the list of MCMC samplers.  This behaviour can be subverted, however, by setting nimbleOptions(MCMCorderPriorSamplesSamplersFirst = FALSE).
#'
#' The prior_samples sampler can be assigned to non-stochastic model nodes (nodes which are not assigned a prior distribution in the model). In fact, it is recommended that nodes being assigned a prior_samples are not provided with a prior distribution in the model, and rather, that these nodes only appear on the right-hand-side of model declaration lines.  In such case that a prior_samples sampler is assigned to a nodes with a prior distribution, the prior distribution will be overridden by the sample values provided to the sampler; however, the node will still be a stochastic node for other purposes, and will contribute to the model joint-density (using the sample values provided relative to the prior distribution), will have an MCMC sampler assigned to it by default, and also may introduce potential for confusion.  In this case, a message is issued at the time of MCMC building.
#'
#' The prior_samples sampler accepts the following control list elements:
#' \itemize{
#' \item \code{samples}. A numeric vector or matrix.  When the \code{target} node is a single scalar-valued node, \code{samples} should be a numeric vector.  When the \code{target} node specifies d > 2 model dimensions, \code{samples} should be a matrix containing d columns.  The \code{samples} control argument is required.
#' \item \code{randomDraws}. A logical argument, specifying whether to use a random draw from \code{samples} on each iteration.  If \code{samples} is a matrix, then a randomly-selected row of the \code{samples} matrix is used.  When \code{FALSE}, sequential values (or sequential matrix rows) are used (default = \code{FALSE}).
#' }
